title: Decode escapes read from a file

blocks.text: The page's `translateEscapes()` does at run time what the compiler does in the last step of processing a text block: it turns written escape sequences into the characters they stand for. Its example is a value read from a file, `Hello\nWorld\tTab` with a real backslash before the `n` and the `t`: 17 characters before, 15 after.

Write `Escapes.decode(String raw)`. `raw` holds escape sequences written out, backslash and all. Return the string with every escape replaced by its character: `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\b`, `\f`, `\s` (a space), `\"`, `\'`, `\\` (one backslash), octal escapes such as `\101` (`A`), and a backslash right before a line break, which removes both and joins the two lines. Each escape is read **once, left to right**, so the `n` in `\\n` is an ordinary letter after a backslash. A backslash followed by anything else is not an escape: throw `IllegalArgumentException`.

cases.says: Written escapes such as \n and \t become a real newline and a real tab.
A written \\ becomes one backslash, and the letter after it stays a letter.
The written \s becomes a single space, as it does in a text block.
A backslash right before a line break (\n or \r\n) removes both, joining the lines, as in a text block.
A backslash before a letter that is no escape makes the call throw IllegalArgumentException.

concepts: translateEscapes() turns written escape sequences into their characters at run time, like the compiler's last step, and refuses an invalid one.
